summary:
Bihār has no state-specific transgender legislation. A trans visitor to the state stands under India's national framework alone, and no source material shows a Bihār-level deviation from the national position.

That national framework was rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in both houses, amending the 2019 Act, and the measure awaits presidential assent. It removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment recognising transgender people as a third gender, and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The amendment also mandates medical certification for identity recognition.

Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their risk. Opposition parties and LGBTQ organisations protested the passage. The government argues the change widens access to welfare benefits; critics say it excludes many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

Recognition for trans visitors and residents across Bihār is therefore governed by the amended national scheme, not by self-declaration. This is the operative baseline for identity documents, welfare eligibility and any interaction with state authorities in the state.

Even before the amendment, the 2014 third gender recognition remained uneven in practice, with continuing discrimination reported in education, healthcare and formal employment. The amendment's effect on that baseline is not separately sourced for Bihār.
tangentialFactors:
India's entry and stay baseline for trans visitors is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity; no same-sex marriage or civil partnership exists, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024, when the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code and omitted the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences the old code carried. Trans people and advocates have reported fear of a rise in assaults as a result.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented elsewhere in India, including a February 2026 Allahabad High Court order granting relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities, and a November 2024 incident in which an openly trans law student was stopped at Chennai International Airport despite producing identification. Comparable accounts exist from railway police in Assam and Kolkata. No source documents an equivalent checkpoint incident in Bihār itself.

Assessments of police conduct diverge nationally. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 judgment in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy; conversion therapy nevertheless continues through clandestine networks.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bihār seeking legal recognition as transgender must satisfy the amended national scheme: recognition is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, and requires medical certification. Self-identification outside those categories no longer secures recognition.

Eligibility for national welfare schemes tied to transgender status runs through that recognition scheme. The government's stated purpose for the amendment is to widen access to such benefits; the practical effect for residents who fall outside the recognised categories is that they are excluded from the scheme's protections.

The Ayushman Bharat health-insurance scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance confirmed that LGBTQ people face no restriction on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. Both are national provisions applying in Bihār; neither has been separately sourced to state-level implementation here.

Recognition and employment protection remain uneven in practice, with discrimination reported in education, healthcare and formal employment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses Bihār specifically. There is no information on Bihār police conduct toward trans people, on transgender welfare boards or state schemes in Bihār, or on the availability of transition-related surgery, housing subsidies or pensions through the state. Whether Bihār operates any state-level welfare machinery comparable to Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra or Odisha is unresolved and not sourced.

The status of presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was unresolved at the time of sourcing; the bill had passed both houses of Parliament but had not been presented as enacted.

Whether the amendment's removal of self-identification has been applied retrospectively to identity documents already issued under the 2019 Act, and how it interacts with the Supreme Court's 2014 third gender judgment, is unresolved in the sources consulted.
